## What you will learn

- What a crop simulation model does, and what an *experiment* (FileX) and its *treatments* are.
- How to run DSSAT on an existing experiment and compare its results with field measurements.
- How the maize model decides when the crop flowers and matures (phenology, thermal time).
- How to change one input at a time (sensitivity analysis) and read the result.
- How to set up the simplest experiment, **potential production**, in which only weather, CO2 and the
  cultivar limit the crop.

The topics follow the first day of the 2018 International Training Program on DSSAT in Chiang Mai
([syllabus](https://github.com/bennyistanto/site/blob/main/docs/blog/20180911-dssat-training-in-chiang-mai-2018.qmd)).
The course used the DSSAT shell and its tools (XBuild, the Sensitivity Analysis tool, GBuild); here each
of those steps is a few lines of Python, using xdssat's modules and the stock DSSAT engine, version 4.8.

## 0. DSSAT and its Cropping System Model

### Where DSSAT comes from

The course opened with the history of crop modelling and of DSSAT. In outline, as its first lecture told it:

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Late 1960s | Crop simulation starts with Dutch (C. T. de Wit) and US researchers, who wanted to predict growth and yield to design management and quantify the effect of weather |
| 1982 to 1993 | The IBSNAT project (International Benchmark Sites Network for Agrotechnology Transfer), based at the University of Hawaii and funded by USAID, builds a network of researchers, data standards and DSSAT itself |
| 1983 | The minimum data set for running crop models is defined (module 2) |
| 1985 to 1986 | DSSAT is named (1985) and first released (1986) with maize, wheat, soybean and peanut. Its models came from CERES-Maize and CERES-Wheat and from SOYGRO and PNUTGRO, each until then a separate program with its own soil, weather and management code |
| December 1993 to October 2014 | ICASA (International Consortium for Agricultural Systems Applications) carries the work on, joining IBSNAT with the Dutch systems effort, and maintains the data standards |
| From 2004 | The Cropping System Model replaces the separate programs with one modular engine [@jones2003] |
| 2012 onwards | The DSSAT Foundation develops and distributes DSSAT ([dssat.net](https://dssat.net/about/)) |

The separate programs were hard to keep compatible, to maintain and to extend to new crops, which the course
gave as the reason DSSAT was created. The Cropping System Model later joined them into one modular engine with
shared soil, weather and management modules [@jones2003], and that engine is what every page of this site runs.

Today DSSAT centres on one program, the Cropping System Model
(CSM): a single Fortran engine built from modules for the weather, the soil (water, nitrogen, carbon,
temperature), the exchange between soil, plant and atmosphere (`SPAM`), management, and a family of plant models
that share one interface [@jones2003]. Counting the source code of the engine used on this site shows how the work
is divided:

```{ojs}
}), "module1-csm-modules")
```

The plant part alone holds ${csmPlants.length} model families, from CERES (cereals) and CROPGRO (grain legumes and
more) to models for potato, sugarcane, cassava and pineapple:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(csmPlants, {header: {plant_model: "Plant model folder", source_files: "Source files"}, layout: "auto", rows: 12})
```

Counted by the module 1 notebook in [DSSAT/dssat-csm-os](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os) at the commit
pinned on this site (folders `Plant`, `Soil`, `SPAM`, `Weather`, `Management`, `InputModule`, `Utilities`,
`CSM_Main`; files ending `.for` or `.f90`).

The same engine serves very different questions. The course listed diagnosing yield gaps, precision agriculture,
water, irrigation and soil fertility management, plant breeding and genotype by environment interactions,
gene-based modelling, yield prediction, and the effects of climate variability and climate change; the DSSAT
Foundation's own list today is similar ([About DSSAT](https://dssat.net/about/)). [Module 6](module6.qmd#applications-and-needs-a-discussion)
returns to these applications and what each one needs.

## 1. A crop model, an experiment, a treatment

DSSAT's Cropping System Model grows a crop one day at a time [@jones2003]. Each day it reads the weather
(radiation, temperature, rain), works out how far the crop has developed, how much it has grown, and how
much water and nitrogen the roots took from each soil layer. Its inputs are the weather, the soil profile,
the cultivar's genetic coefficients and the management: planting, irrigation, fertilizer.

A useful way to think about what limits a crop is the hierarchy of **production levels**
[@vanittersum1997]. *Potential* yield is set by radiation, temperature, CO2 and the cultivar alone.
*Attainable* (water- and nutrient-limited) yield is lower where water or nitrogen run short. *Actual* yield
is lower still where weeds, pests and diseases reduce it. DSSAT simulates the first two levels; this
module starts with real treatments and ends with the potential.

The example is a maize experiment from Gainesville, Florida, in 1982 (`UFGA8201`, cultivar McCurdy 84aa),
one of the example experiments shipped with DSSAT [@csmdata]. It has six **treatments**: every combination
of three water regimes and two nitrogen rates. In the experiment file each treatment is a row that picks one
*level* of each factor (cultivar, field, initial conditions, planting, irrigation, fertilizer, simulation
controls).

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(treatments, {header: {TRNO: "Treatment", TNAME: "Name in the FileX", water: "Water", nitrogen: "Nitrogen"}, layout: "auto"})
```

## 2. Running the model and checking it against the field

The notebook copies the experiment, its weather and soil files and the field measurements into a short
work folder and runs the engine on all six treatments. The engine writes one summary row per treatment and
daily time series. The field data come in two files: end-of-season values (FileA) and samples taken during
the season (FileT).

```{ojs}
viewof finalVar = Inputs.select([...new Set(final.map(d => d.variable))], {label: "Variable", value: "Grain yield, kg/ha"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = final.filter(d => d.variable === finalVar);
  const hi = d3.max(rows, d => Math.max(d.simulated, d.observed)) * 1.08;
  const lo = finalVar.includes("DAP") ? d3.min(rows, d => Math.min(d.simulated, d.observed)) * 0.95 : 0;
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: Math.min(W, 520), height: 420, marginLeft: 60,
    x: {label: `Observed: ${finalVar}`, domain: [lo, hi], grid: true},
    y: {label: `Simulated: ${finalVar}`, domain: [lo, hi], grid: true},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["rainfed", "irrigated", "vegetative stress"]},
    symbol: {legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line([[lo, lo], [hi, hi]], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot(rows.map(d => ({...d, water: treatments.find(t => t.TRNO === d.TRNO).water,
                                nitrogen: treatments.find(t => t.TRNO === d.TRNO).nitrogen + " N"})),
        {x: "observed", y: "simulated", stroke: "water", symbol: "nitrogen", r: 6, strokeWidth: 2, tip: true,
         channels: {treatment: "treatment"}})
    ]
  }), `module1-sim-vs-obs-${finalVar.replace(/[^a-z]+/gi, "-")}`);
}
```

```{ojs}
yieldRows = final.filter(d => d.variable === "Grain yield, kg/ha")
```

Across the six treatments, simulated grain yield ranges from ${fmt.int(d3.min(yieldRows, d => d.simulated))} to ${fmt.int(d3.max(yieldRows, d => d.simulated))} kg/ha against ${fmt.int(d3.min(yieldRows, d => d.observed))} to ${fmt.int(d3.max(yieldRows, d => d.observed))} kg/ha measured. The model ranks the treatments the way the field did: the rainfed plots yield least, and the
irrigated high-N plot most. It does not separate the two rainfed treatments: with too little water,
extra nitrogen makes no simulated difference to grain.

### Growth during the season

Pick a variable; the lines are the daily simulation, the dots the field samples.

```{ojs}
viewof gVar = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Leaf area index", "LAID"], ["Tops weight, kg/ha", "CWAD"], ["Grain weight, kg/ha", "GWAD"]]), {value: "CWAD", label: "Variable"})
viewof gTrt = Inputs.checkbox(treatments.map(d => d.TRNO), {value: [1, 4, 6], label: "Treatments", format: t => trtName.get(t)})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 380, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: gVar, grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: gTrt.map(t => trtName.get(t))},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(gsim.filter(d => gTrt.includes(d.TRNO)), {x: "DAP", y: gVar, stroke: d => trtName.get(d.TRNO), tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(gobs.filter(d => gTrt.includes(d.TRNO) && d[gVar] != null), {x: "DAP", y: gVar, fill: d => trtName.get(d.TRNO), r: 4, tip: true})
  ]
}), `module1-growth-${gVar}`)
```

GBuild's *Statistics* option reports how far the simulation is from the samples. The notebook computes the
same two numbers: the root mean square error (RMSE, in the variable's units) and Willmott's index of
agreement *d*, which is 1 for a perfect match and has no units [@willmott1981]. For \(n\) pairs of observed
\(O_i\) and simulated \(S_i\) values, with \(\bar O\) the mean of the observations:

\[
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (S_i - O_i)^2} \\[4pt]
d = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (S_i - O_i)^2}{\sum_i \left(|S_i - \bar O| + |O_i - \bar O|\right)^2}
\end{gathered}
\]

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(stats.map(d => ({...d, treatment: trtName.get(d.TRNO), variable: ({LAID: "LAI", CWAD: "Tops, kg/ha", GWAD: "Grain, kg/ha"})[d.variable]})),
  {columns: ["treatment", "variable", "n", "rmse", "d"], header: {n: "Samples", rmse: "RMSE", d: "Willmott d"},
   format: {rmse: d => d.toFixed(2), d: d => d.toFixed(2)}, layout: "auto", rows: 18})
```

## 3. Phenology: when does the crop flower?

**Development** (moving through life stages) is not the same as **growth** (adding mass). A crop that
develops fast has a short life; that does not make it bigger. Temperature drives development in all crops;
day length matters for some cultivars.

CERES-Maize counts development in **thermal time**, degree-days above a base temperature. Each day adds
`DTT` degree-days; each phase ends when its requirement is met. For maize: emergence, the end of the
juvenile phase after `P1` degree-days, a floral induction phase that day length can slow (`P2`), tassel
initiation, silking, grain filling for `P5` degree-days, and maturity.

How one day's `DTT` is computed is set in the engine's Fortran
([`MZ_PHENOL.for`, lines 437-517](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CERES-Maize/MZ_PHENOL.for#L437)).
The base temperature `TBASE` is ${eco.TBASE} °C here and the optimum `TOPT` is ${eco.TOPT} °C; both come
from the ecotype file `MZCER048.ECO`. Try it: the function below is a direct port of the air-temperature branches
(the engine uses an estimated soil temperature while the plant has 10 leaves or fewer, when its growing
point is still near the ground; that branch is left out here). With \(T_{base}\), the optimum \(T_{opt}\) and the
day's \(T_{max}\) and \(T_{min}\):

\[
\begin{gathered}
DTT =
\begin{cases}
0 & T_{max} < T_{base} \\
T_{opt} - T_{base} & T_{min} > T_{opt} \\
DTT_{hourly} & T_{min} < T_{base} \text{ or } T_{max} > T_{opt} \\
\dfrac{T_{max} + T_{min}}{2} - T_{base} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\[6pt]
DTT_{hourly} = \frac{1}{24}\sum_{h=1}^{24} \left(\min\left(\max(T_h, T_{base}), T_{opt}\right) - T_{base}\right)
\end{gathered}
\]

with hourly temperatures from a sine curve,
\(T_h = \frac{T_{max} + T_{min}}{2} + \frac{T_{max} - T_{min}}{2}\,\sin\!\left(\frac{3.14\,h}{12}\right)\). A phase ends
on the day its sum reaches the cultivar's requirement, \(\sum DTT \ge P1\) for the juvenile phase.

```{ojs}
function dtt(tmax, tmin, tbase = eco.TBASE, dopt = eco.TOPT) {
  if (tmax < tbase) return 0;
  if (tmin > dopt) return dopt - tbase;
  if (tmin < tbase || tmax > dopt) {
    let s = 0;
    for (let i = 1; i <= 24; i++) {
      let th = (tmax + tmin) / 2 + (tmax - tmin) / 2 * Math.sin(3.14 / 12 * i);
      th = Math.min(Math.max(th, tbase), dopt);
      s += (th - tbase) / 24;
    }
    return s;
  }
  return (tmax + tmin) / 2 - tbase;
}
viewof tRange = Inputs.range([0, 25], {step: 1, value: 12, label: "Daily range Tmax - Tmin, °C"})
```

```{ojs}
dttRows = d3.range(-5, 46, 0.5).flatMap(tm => [
  {tmean: tm, dtt: dtt(tm + tRange / 2, tm - tRange / 2), rule: `Engine rule, range ${tRange} °C`},
  {tmean: tm, dtt: Math.max(0, tm - eco.TBASE), rule: "Simple mean - TBASE, no cap"}])
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 640), height: 330, marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "Daily mean temperature, °C", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Thermal time added that day, °C-day", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([eco.TBASE, eco.TOPT], {stroke: "#bbb", strokeDasharray: "3,3"}),
    Plot.text([{x: eco.TBASE, t: "TBASE"}, {x: eco.TOPT, t: "TOPT"}], {x: "x", y: 30, text: "t", dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", fill: "#666"}),
    Plot.lineY(dttRows, {x: "tmean", y: "dtt", stroke: "rule", strokeWidth: 2, tip: true})
  ]
}), "module1-thermal-time-function")
```

With a wide daily range, part of the day is below `TBASE` or above `TOPT` even when the mean is not; the
hourly sine curve gives those hours less (or no) thermal time, so the curve bends before it reaches the
cap. Above `TOPT` the rate does not fall: the model has no penalty for heat in this function.

Over the 1982 season, the thermal time adds up like this (air-temperature branches only, so slightly
different from the engine's own sum early in the season). The vertical lines are the stage changes the
engine simulated for treatment 4:

```{ojs}
stageName = new Map([[0, "planting"], [1, "emergence"], [2, "end of juvenile phase"], [3, "tassel initiation"], [4, "end of leaf growth, silking"], [5, "start of effective grain fill"], [6, "end of grain fill"]])
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 330, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {type: "utc", label: "Date, 1982"},
  y: {label: "Cumulative thermal time from planting, °C-day", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(weather, {x: d => new Date(d.date), y: "GDD_cum", stroke: "#2a7f62", strokeWidth: 2, tip: true}),
    Plot.ruleX(stages, {x: d => new Date(d.date), stroke: "#d9822b"}),
    Plot.text(stages, {x: d => new Date(d.date), y: (d, i) => 2600 - i * 380, text: d => `${stageName.get(d.stage)} (DAP ${d.DAP})`, dx: 4, textAnchor: "start", fontSize: 10, fill: "#333", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.dot(stages, {x: d => new Date(d.date), y: "GDD_cum", fill: "#d9822b", tip: true})
  ]
}), "module1-thermal-time-1982")
```

::: {.source-note}
Stage numbers are the PlantGro `GSTD` values of treatment 4. For CERES-Maize `GSTD` is the phenology
stage `ISTAGE` once the plant has leaves (`MZ_GROSUB.for:1847-1851`); each line marks the day a stage
begins, named after the stage comments in `MZ_PHENOL.for` (lines 647-875). McCurdy 84aa: P1 = ${coef[0].P1} °C-day, P2 = ${coef[0].P2} d/h,
P5 = ${coef[0].P5} °C-day (engine's `MZCER048.CUL`).
:::

### Temperature responses in CROPGRO

CERES-Maize uses one base temperature and one optimum. CROPGRO, the model of the grain legumes in module 2, uses a
four-point function instead: no development below a base `TB`, a rise to a first optimum `TO1`, a plateau to a
second optimum `TO2`, and a decline to zero at a maximum `TM`,

\[
f(T) =
\begin{cases}
0 & T \le T_B \text{ or } T \ge T_M \\
\dfrac{T - T_B}{T_{O1} - T_B} & T_B < T < T_{O1} \\
1 & T_{O1} \le T \le T_{O2} \\
1 - \dfrac{T - T_{O2}}{T_M - T_{O2}} & T_{O2} < T < T_M
\end{cases}
\]

([`UTILS.for:353-358`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Utilities/UTILS.for#L353), curve type `LIN`, called in
[`PHENOL.for:237`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CROPGRO/PHENOL.for#L237)). Soybean's species file sets one function for each of
three phases of development:

```{ojs}
function curvLin(x, xb, x1, x2, xm) {
  if (x <= xb || x >= xm) return 0;
  if (x < x1) return (x - xb) / (x1 - xb);
  if (x <= x2) return 1;
  return 1 - (x - x2) / (xm - x2);
}
viewof tPhase = Inputs.radio(tfun.map(d => d.phase), {value: tfun[0].phase, label: "Phase"})
```

```{ojs}
tf = tfun.find(d => d.phase === tPhase)
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 640), height: 300, marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "Hourly temperature, °C", domain: [-5, 50], grid: true},
  y: {label: "Relative rate of development", domain: [0, 1.05], grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: tfun.map(d => d.phase), range: ["#3f7a34", "#f2a33a", "#4a6fa5"]},
  marks: [
    ...tfun.map(p => Plot.line(d3.range(-5, 50.1, 0.25).map(x => [x, curvLin(x, p.TB, p.TO1, p.TO2, p.TM)]), {stroke: () => p.phase, strokeWidth: p.phase === tPhase ? 3 : 1, strokeOpacity: p.phase === tPhase ? 1 : 0.4})),
    Plot.dot([tf.TB, tf.TO1, tf.TO2, tf.TM].map((x, i) => ({x, y: i === 1 || i === 2 ? 1 : 0, k: ["TB", "TO1", "TO2", "TM"][i]})), {x: "x", y: "y", r: 5, fill: "#222", tip: true, channels: {point: "k"}})
  ]
}), "module1-cropgro-temperature")
```

::: {.source-note}
Values from the engine's `SBGRO048.SPE` (phenology parameters): TB ${tf.TB}, TO1 ${tf.TO1}, TO2 ${tf.TO2}, TM ${tf.TM} °C for this phase. CROPGRO applies the function to hourly temperatures.
:::

## 4. Potential production

Now the simplest experiment: water and nitrogen are not simulated at all (`WATER` and `NITRO` switched to
`N` in the simulation controls), so only weather, CO2 and the cultivar limit growth. In the DSSAT shell
this is a new FileX made in XBuild. In the notebook it is built from treatment 4 of UFGA8201 with
`filex.build_filex`, keeping the same field, cultivar and planting date. With the water switch off, DSSAT
skips the soil water balance
([`SPAM.for:269`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/SPAM/SPAM.for#L269));
with the N switch off, CERES-Maize has no N stress
([`MZ_GROSUB.for:2059`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CERES-Maize/MZ_GROSUB.for#L2059)).

```{ojs}
potM = potential.find(d => d.scenario.endsWith("CO2 M"))
potD = potential.find(d => d.scenario.endsWith("CO2 D"))
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 360, marginLeft: 230,
  x: {label: "Grain yield, kg/ha", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["potential", "UFGA8201 treatments", "observed"], range: ["#2a7f62", "#9bb8ad", "#d9822b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(potential, {y: "scenario", x: "HWAM", fill: "group", tip: true, channels: {"share of potential": d => fmt.pct(d.share_of_potential)}, sort: {y: "-x"}}),
    Plot.dot(potential.filter(d => d.HWAM_obs != null), {y: "scenario", x: "HWAM_obs", fill: () => "observed", r: 5, stroke: "white", tip: true}),
    Plot.ruleX([potM.HWAM], {stroke: "#2a7f62", strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
  ]
}), "module1-potential-vs-treatments")
```

The potential run (measured CO2) gives ${fmt.int(potM.HWAM)} kg/ha. The irrigated high-N treatment
reached ${fmt.pct(potential.find(d => d.scenario.startsWith("T4")).share_of_potential)} of it in the model;
the rainfed treatments ${fmt.pct(potential.find(d => d.scenario.startsWith("T1")).share_of_potential)}.
Water, not nitrogen, made the largest difference in this season.

**CO2.** DSSAT can take CO2 from a measured series (option `M`, Mauna Loa) or use a fixed value (option `D`,
380 ppm from `CO2048.WDA`), see
[`CO2VAL.for`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Weather/CO2VAL.for#L5).
The 1982 series averages ${fmt.d1(potM.CO2_mean)} ppm over the season; with 380 ppm the potential yield is ${fmt.int(potD.HWAM)} kg/ha, ${fmt.pct(potD.HWAM / potM.HWAM - 1)} more: a small effect for a ${fmt.int(380 - potM.CO2_mean)} ppm difference.

## 5. Sensitivity analysis: one thing at a time

The Sensitivity Analysis tool changes one input and reruns. All runs below are potential production, so
that water and nitrogen do not blur the effect.

### Cultivars

Six maize cultivars from the engine's cultivar file, from a short to a long juvenile phase (`P1`):

```{ojs}
viewof culPick = Inputs.checkbox(sensCul.map(d => d.var), {value: sensCul.map(d => d.var), label: "Cultivars",
  format: v => { const c = sensCul.find(d => d.var === v); return `${c.name} (P1 ${c.P1})`; }})
viewof culVar = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Leaf area index", "LAID"], ["Grain weight, kg/ha", "GWAD"], ["Tops weight, kg/ha", "CWAD"]]), {value: "LAID", label: "Variable"})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 360, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: culVar, grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: culPick.map(v => sensCul.find(d => d.var === v).name)},
  marks: [Plot.lineY(sensCulG.filter(d => culPick.includes(d.var)), {x: "DAP", y: culVar, stroke: d => sensCul.find(c => c.var === d.var).name, tip: true})]
}), `module1-cultivars-${culVar}`)
```

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(sensCul, {columns: ["name", "P1", "P2", "P5", "G2", "G3", "anthesis_dap", "maturity_dap", "HWAM", "LAIX"],
  header: {name: "Cultivar", anthesis_dap: "Anthesis, DAP", maturity_dap: "Maturity, DAP", HWAM: "Yield, kg/ha", LAIX: "Max LAI"}, layout: "auto"})
```

A longer juvenile phase delays anthesis (from ${d3.min(sensCul, d => d.anthesis_dap)} to ${d3.max(sensCul, d => d.anthesis_dap)} days after planting here) and builds more leaf area, but the highest yield is
not the latest cultivar: yield also depends on grain filling (`P5`, `G2`, `G3`), and McCurdy 84aa has the
longest grain filling of the six. A potential yield like this belongs to a cultivar at one place in one
year; it is not a fixed property of the cultivar.

### Planting date

Pick a planting date; 26 February is the experiment's own date, the others follow in steps of two weeks.

```{ojs}
viewof pdPick = Inputs.range([0, sensPd.length - 1], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "Planting", format: i => sensPd[i].planting})
```

```{ojs}
pdSel = sensPd[pdPick]
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 340, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Leaf area index", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(sensPdG, {x: "DAP", y: "LAID", z: "planting", stroke: "#ccc"}),
    Plot.lineY(sensPdG.filter(d => d.planting === pdSel.planting), {x: "DAP", y: "LAID", stroke: "#2a7f62", strokeWidth: 3, tip: true})
  ]
}), `module1-planting-${pdSel.planting.replace(" ", "")}`)
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 640), height: 300, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Planting date", domain: sensPd.map(d => d.planting)},
  y: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(sensPd.flatMap(d => [{p: d.planting, v: d.anthesis_dap, k: "anthesis"}, {p: d.planting, v: d.maturity_dap, k: "maturity"}]), {x: "p", y: "v", stroke: "k", marker: "dot", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot([pdSel], {x: "planting", y: "maturity_dap", r: 8, stroke: "#d9822b", strokeWidth: 2})
  ]
}), "module1-planting-dates-phenology")
```

Planted ${pdSel.planting}: anthesis after ${pdSel.anthesis_dap} days, maturity after ${pdSel.maturity_dap} days, potential yield ${fmt.int(pdSel.HWAM)} kg/ha; mean temperature over the season ${fmt.d1(pdSel.season_tmean)} °C and mean radiation ${fmt.d1(pdSel.season_srad)} MJ/m²/day. Later plantings grow in warmer
weather, so they accumulate thermal time faster and mature sooner. Yield does not follow a simple line
over the six dates; the notebook has the daily weather to dig into why.

### One genetic coefficient

Change `P1` (thermal time of the juvenile phase) or `P5` (thermal time of grain filling) of McCurdy 84aa.
The notebook writes a copy of the cultivar file with the new value into each run folder; the engine reads
the local file first, so its own file is never changed.

```{ojs}
viewof coefPick = Inputs.radio(["P1", "P5"], {value: "P1", label: "Coefficient"})
```

```{ojs}
coefVals = sensCoef.filter(d => d.coefficient === coefPick).map(d => d.value)
viewof coefVal = Inputs.range([d3.min(coefVals), d3.max(coefVals)], {step: coefVals[1] - coefVals[0], value: coefPick === "P1" ? 250 : 950, label: `${coefPick}, °C-day`})
```

```{ojs}
coefSel = sensCoef.find(d => d.coefficient === coefPick && d.value === coefVal)
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 340, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Grain weight, kg/ha", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(sensCoefG.filter(d => d.coefficient === coefPick), {x: "DAP", y: "GWAD", z: "value", stroke: "#ccc"}),
    Plot.lineY(sensCoefG.filter(d => d.coefficient === coefPick && d.value === coefVal), {x: "DAP", y: "GWAD", stroke: "#2a7f62", strokeWidth: 3, tip: true})
  ]
}), `module1-${coefPick}-${coefVal}-grain`)
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 640), height: 300, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: `${coefPick}, °C-day`, grid: true},
  y: {label: "Potential grain yield, kg/ha", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(sensCoef.filter(d => d.coefficient === coefPick), {x: "value", y: "HWAM", stroke: "#2a7f62", marker: "dot", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot([coefSel], {x: "value", y: "HWAM", r: 8, stroke: "#d9822b", strokeWidth: 2, tip: true})
  ]
}), `module1-${coefPick}-response`)
```

With ${coefPick} = ${coefVal}: anthesis ${coefSel?.anthesis_dap} days after planting, maturity ${coefSel?.maturity_dap}, potential yield ${fmt.int(coefSel?.HWAM)} kg/ha. `P5` lengthens grain
filling without moving anthesis, and yield rises with it. `P1` moves both dates, and yield is highest at
P1 = ${p1Best.value} with ${fmt.int(p1Best.HWAM)} kg/ha, not at either end of the range; the notebook's daily
weather is the place to look for why.

```{ojs}
p1Best = sensCoef.filter(d => d.coefficient === "P1").reduce((a, b) => b.HWAM > a.HWAM ? b : a)
```

## From one field to a grid: xdssat

Every experiment above is one field. xdssat runs the same engine, unchanged, for every 0.1° weather cell of a
region, one simulation per cell, season and water regime. In the [rice case study](../java/index.qmd) that is
${fmt.int(gCells.length)} cells of Java over 30 years (current run: ${gSummary.current_run}). Phenology is where the
grid shows its first pattern: the same cultivar, planted by the same rule, takes longer to mature where nights are
cooler, because thermal time accumulates more slowly (section 3).

```{ojs}
import {cellFeatures, adminMarks} from "../assets/js/dl.js"
gCells = FileAttachment("../java/data/grid_cells.csv").csv({typed: true})
gOutline = FileAttachment("../java/data/java_outline.geojson").json()
gProv = FileAttachment("../java/data/provinces.geojson").json()
gDist = FileAttachment("../java/data/districts.geojson").json()
gSummary = FileAttachment("../java/data/summary.json").json()
gMapW = Math.min(width, 960)
```

```{ojs}
viewof g1Var = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Days from planting to maturity", "len_wet_irrigated"], ["Mean season minimum temperature, °C", "tmina_wet_irrigated"]]), {value: "len_wet_irrigated", label: "Map"})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: gMapW, height: Math.round(gMapW * 0.42),
  projection: {type: "mercator", domain: gOutline},
  color: {type: "linear", scheme: g1Var.startsWith("len") ? "YlOrBr" : "RdYlBu", reverse: g1Var.startsWith("tmin"), legend: true,
          label: g1Var.startsWith("len") ? "Irrigated wet-season rice: days to maturity (1991-2020 mean)" : "Mean season Tmin, °C"},
  marks: [
    Plot.geo(gProv, {fill: "#f1f1f1", clip: true}),
    Plot.geo(cellFeatures(gCells.filter(d => d[g1Var] != null)).features, Plot.centroid({fill: d => d.properties[g1Var], tip: true,
      title: d => `${d.properties.lat.toFixed(1)}, ${d.properties.lon.toFixed(1)}: ${fmt.d1(d.properties.len_wet_irrigated)} days, Tmin ${fmt.d1(d.properties.tmina_wet_irrigated)} °C`})),
    ...adminMarks(Plot, gProv, gDist)
  ]
}), `module1-grid-${g1Var}`)
```

```{ojs}
g1 = gCells.filter(d => d.len_wet_irrigated != null && d.tmina_wet_irrigated != null)
g1r = (() => { const x = g1.map(d => d.tmina_wet_irrigated), y = g1.map(d => d.len_wet_irrigated); const mx = d3.mean(x), my = d3.mean(y);
  return d3.sum(x, (v, i) => (v - mx) * (y[i] - my)) / Math.sqrt(d3.sum(x, v => (v - mx) ** 2) * d3.sum(y, v => (v - my) ** 2)); })()
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 560), height: 300, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Mean season minimum temperature, °C", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Days from planting to maturity", grid: true},
  marks: [Plot.dot(g1, {x: "tmina_wet_irrigated", y: "len_wet_irrigated", r: 2, fill: "#3f7a34", fillOpacity: 0.5, tip: true})]
}), "module1-grid-length-vs-tmin")
```

Across the ${fmt.int(g1.length)} cells with irrigated wet-season rice, season length and night temperature correlate at r = ${g1r.toFixed(2)}, from ${fmt.int(d3.min(g1, d => d.len_wet_irrigated))} to ${fmt.int(d3.max(g1, d => d.len_wet_irrigated))} days. The [case study's Science page](../java/science.qmd) shows what that does to the simulated yield.

## Self-test

1. Which treatment of UFGA8201 is closest to potential production, and why is it not exactly equal?
2. The model gives the same grain yield to both rainfed treatments. What does that tell you about which
   factor limited them?
3. In the cultivar comparison, why does the cultivar with the most leaf area not give the most grain?
4. Change the CO2 option in the notebook to `W` (CO2 from the weather file). What happens, and why?
5. Add a planting date in July in the notebook. Predict anthesis and maturity first, then run it.
